A Note on This Topic's Scope
Blood — Your Body's Delivery and Defense System

items: Blood is the only liquid tissue you have, and that is the entire point: it must reach everywhere, fast.
Everything it does falls under two headings — transport (oxygen, nutrients, hormones, heat, waste) and defence (against infection, and against leaks).
It is a suspension, not a solution: cells floating in plasma. Spin it in a tube and it separates into layers you can actually see.
The final third of this topic — hemostasis — is one of the most beautifully controlled systems in the body: it must clot fast enough to save you, but never so readily that it kills you.
Two jobs: transport and defence. Every fact in this topic serves one or the other.
About 8% of body weight — roughly 5 litres in an average adult.
By volume: ~55% plasma, ~45% cells (overwhelmingly red cells).
Plasma = the liquid part with clotting factors. Serum = what is left after clotting, so it lacks fibrinogen and the factors used up.
Simple way to hold it: serum = plasma − clotting factors.
Donating a unit of blood removes roughly a tenth of your volume — replaced within a day or two, though the red cells take weeks.
A blood sample stands and separates into a clear yellow top layer and a dark base: you are literally seeing plasma and cells.

blocks.x: Blood is the only tissue in your body that is liquid, and that's exactly the point — it needs to flow everywhere, fast, carrying supplies in and waste out, while also standing ready to fight off invaders and plug any leaks. Everything in this topic ultimately serves one of those two jobs: transport, or defense.

blocks.name: Two major functions of blood
blocks.def: Transport (of gases, nutrients, waste products, and hormones) and defense (via antibodies and leucocytes).

blocks.name: Blood as a percentage of body weight
blocks.def: About 8% of normal body weight.

blocks.cap: Whole blood: 55% plasma, 45% cells — and what each fraction contains.

blocks.name: Composition of blood by volume
blocks.def: 55% plasma (the fluid part) and 45% cells — mainly erythrocytes (red blood cells), since they make up 99% of the cellular portion. This 45% figure has a specific name: the hematocrit.

blocks.name: Plasma
blocks.def: The fluid portion of blood — a solvent for K+, Na+, Ca2+, Cl-, HCO3-, and other inorganic and organic ions. Plasma clots on standing if whole blood is left alone.

blocks.name: Serum
blocks.def: What remains after whole blood is allowed to clot and the clot is removed. Serum has the SAME composition as plasma, EXCEPT it lacks fibrinogen and clotting factors V and VIII, since these were consumed in forming the clot. Memory hook: Serum = Plasma minus the clotting factors.

items: Albumin — the most abundant. It is the body's sponge, holding water inside vessels by osmotic pressure, and the general-purpose taxi for drugs, hormones and fatty acids.
Globulins — transport proteins and, crucially, antibodies.
Fibrinogen and clotting factors — the raw material of a clot.
Together they also buffer pH and give blood its viscosity.
In severe liver disease or malnutrition, albumin falls and water leaks out of the vessels into the tissues — the swollen legs and distended belly of kwashiorkor are albumin failing at its sponge job.
Because albumin carries drugs, a low albumin level can make a normal dose behave like an overdose.

blocks.name: Albumin
blocks.def: A plasma protein produced by the liver — the most abundant plasma protein, and the main contributor to oncotic pressure (which keeps fluid from leaking out of capillary walls).

blocks.name: Globulins
blocks.def: A family of plasma proteins involved in various transport and immune functions.

blocks.name: Fibrinogen and clotting factors
blocks.def: Plasma proteins specifically dedicated to blood clotting — these are exactly what's missing from serum.

blocks.name: Functions of plasma proteins (overview)
blocks.def: Maintaining oncotic pressure (via impermeability across capillary walls), contributing to the buffering capacity of blood (accounting for about 15% of blood's buffering), and transporting hormones, drugs, and metabolites through the circulation.

items: A red cell is a specialist stripped bare: no nucleus, no mitochondria — just a bag of haemoglobin, maximising cargo space.
Its biconcave disc shape gives more surface area for gas exchange and enough flexibility to squeeze through capillaries narrower than itself.
No mitochondria means it cannot consume the oxygen it carries — an elegant piece of design.
The trade-off: no nucleus means no repair, so it lives about 120 days and is then removed by the spleen.
Haematocrit (PCV) = the percentage of blood volume that is red cells. The indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC) simply describe average cell size and haemoglobin content — which is how anaemias are classified.
Production moves through life: yolk sac → liver and spleen → red bone marrow, and is driven by erythropoietin from the kidney in response to low oxygen.
This is why kidney disease causes anaemia — less erythropoietin, so less signal to make red cells.
It is also why living at altitude, or training there, raises red cell count: less oxygen → more erythropoietin → more cells.
The spleen's role explains why old or damaged cells are cleared there, and why spleen problems show up in blood counts.

blocks.x: ▶️Red Blood Cells (Erythrocytes) Concept MapVideo · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: Erythrocyte functions
blocks.def: Transport (via hemoglobin, mainly of oxygen) and buffering (about 50% of blood's total buffering capacity comes from red cells) — red cells also contain carbonic anhydrase, the enzyme that converts CO2 into HCO3- for transport back to the lungs.

blocks.name: RBC shape and size
blocks.def: Biconcave disc shape, about 8.3 cubic micrometers, roughly 7-5 micrometers thick, 2 micrometers at the rim. The biconcave shape allows the cell to VARY its shape considerably (squeezing through tiny capillaries) without rupturing.

blocks.name: Normal RBC count
blocks.def: About 5.4 million/microliter in males, 4.7 million/microliter in females. Varies with age (highest in newborns, lowest at 4-11 months of age) and is higher at high altitude (where the body compensates for lower oxygen availability).

blocks.title: Next up — the numbers, and what each one means

items: Do not memorise these as loose figures. Each index answers one specific question.
Haematocrit — what fraction of blood is cells? Hb concentration — how much oxygen-carrying protein is there?
MCV — how big is the average cell? MCH / MCHC — how much haemoglobin is inside it?
This is precisely how anaemias are classified: MCV sorts them into small, normal or large-celled, which points straight at the cause.

blocks.name: Hematocrit (PCV, Packed Cell Volume)
blocks.def: Tells you the volume percentage of blood occupied by cells, affected by fluid content. Normal: about 47% in males, 42% in females. HIGH hematocrit can indicate dehydration (less plasma volume, relatively more concentrated cells).

blocks.name: Normal hemoglobin concentration
blocks.def: Men: 13.8 to 18.2 g/dL. Women: 12.1 to 15.1 g/dL.

blocks.name: Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)
blocks.def: A derived index (not measured directly) reflecting the average SIZE of red blood cells: MCV = (Hematocrit × 10) ÷ RBC count. Normal value approximately 87 fL. MCV > 95 indicates macrocytes (abnormally large cells); MCV < 80 indicates microcytes (abnormally small cells, often a sign of iron deficiency).

blocks.name: Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH)
blocks.def: A derived index reflecting the average AMOUNT of hemoglobin per red cell: MCH = (Hb × 10) ÷ RBC count. Normal value approximately 29 pg. MCH < 25 indicates hypochromic cells (pale, hemoglobin-poor) — often another indicator of iron deficiency.

blocks.name: Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration (MCHC)
blocks.def: A derived index reflecting the CONCENTRATION of hemoglobin within each red cell: MCHC = (Hb × 100) ÷ Hematocrit. Normal value approximately 34 g/dL.

blocks.name: Sex difference in RBC indices after puberty
blocks.def: From around age 13 onward (puberty), females have LOWER RBC count, hemoglobin, and PCV than males — largely attributable to the hormonal changes and blood loss patterns that begin at puberty.

blocks.title: Next up — where red cells are made, and what controls it

items: Production migrates through life: yolk sac → liver and spleen → red bone marrow.
Reticulocytes are newly released, not-quite-finished cells — so a high count means the marrow is working hard.
Erythropoietin from the kidney is the controller, released when tissue oxygen falls.
It is a textbook negative-feedback loop (Topic 02): low oxygen → EPO → more red cells → oxygen restored → EPO falls.

blocks.name: RBC production sites — before birth
blocks.def: During embryonic life, RBCs are produced in the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes.

blocks.name: RBC production sites — after birth
blocks.def: Produced in bone marrow. In all bones until about age 5; then production shifts to long bones (which become progressively fatty) until about age 20; after that, production is confined to membranous bones plus the humerus and femur.

blocks.name: <term d="The process of making new red blood cells.">Erythropoiesis</term> (RBC maturation sequence)
blocks.def: Starts from a common stem cell (progenitor), progressing through: proerythroblast → basophil erythroblast → polychromatophil erythroblast → orthochromatic erythroblast (late normoblast) → reticulocyte → mature erythrocyte.

blocks.name: Reticulocytes
blocks.def: The immediate precursor to mature erythrocytes, normally making up about 1% of circulating red cells. An INCREASED reticulocyte count signals increased RBC production — a useful clinical marker of active erythropoiesis (e.g., after blood loss or in response to treatment for anemia).

blocks.name: Erythropoietin
blocks.def: The <term d="A chemical messenger released into the blood that acts on distant target tissues.">hormone</term> that stimulates RBC production, released in response to reduced tissue oxygenation. About 90-95% comes from the kidney, 5-10% from the liver. Erythropoietin stimulates the formation of proerythroblasts and their subsequent maturation.

blocks.name: Conditions causing low tissue oxygenation (triggering erythropoietin release)
blocks.def: Reduced blood volume, anemia (low hemoglobin), reduced blood flow (as in cardiac failure), and pulmonary disease (ventilation/perfusion mismatch) — anything that reduces oxygen delivery to tissues triggers this feedback loop.

items: Making red cells needs supplies. Remove any one and you get a specific, recognisable anaemia.
B₁₂ and folate are needed for DNA synthesis — without them cells divide poorly and come out too large (megaloblastic).
Pernicious anaemia is B₁₂ deficiency caused by lack of intrinsic factor, not lack of B₁₂ in the diet.
Iron is needed for haemoglobin itself — too little and the cells come out small and pale.
Quick hook: B₁₂/folate → big cells; iron → small cells.

blocks.name: Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) in RBC formation
blocks.def: Needed for DNA synthesis; since RBCs are being formed rapidly, they need a lot of B12. Lack of B12 causes abnormally big cells (megaloblasts), because DNA production fails while RNA production continues, leading to excess cell constituents relative to divisions — resulting in bigger, fragile, abnormal cells. This causes a form of anemia called pernicious anemia.

blocks.name: Pernicious anemia
blocks.def: Occurs even with a normal dietary intake of B12, because ABSORPTION of B12 is abnormal, due to atrophic gastric mucosa producing abnormal gastric juice. Intrinsic factor, normally secreted by parietal cells (absent in pernicious anemia), must bind B12 to make it absorbable and protect it from enzymatic breakdown. The body's B12 store, held in the liver, can last a year or longer even with defective absorption, which is why the deficiency can take a long time to become apparent.

blocks.name: Folic acid in RBC formation
blocks.def: Also required for DNA formation; deficiency likewise produces a form of pernicious (megaloblastic) anemia, similar in appearance to B12 deficiency.

blocks.title: Next up — iron, the mineral the body refuses to waste

items: Iron is unusual: the body has no way to excrete it deliberately. It can only control how much it absorbs.
Transferrin transports it; ferritin stores it.
Absorption is regulated by need — and helped by vitamin C, hindered by tea, coffee and phytates.
Because there is no exit, iron overload damages organs — the reason iron supplements are not harmless extras.

blocks.name: Total body iron and its distribution
blocks.def: About 4 grams total: 65% in hemoglobin, 4% in myoglobin, and 5-30% stored in the liver (as ferritin and hemosiderin). Iron is also needed for cytochrome oxidase and catalase, beyond just hemoglobin.

blocks.name: Iron absorption chemistry
blocks.def: Iron is absorbed in the Fe2+ (ferrous) form, but dietary iron is mostly Fe3+ (ferric) — gastric secretions form soluble complexes with Fe3+, converting it to the absorbable Fe2+ form.

blocks.name: Inhibitors of iron absorption
blocks.def: Oxalates, phosphates, and phytic acid — these complex with iron and make it insoluble, reducing absorption. Partial gastrectomy also lowers iron absorption (less gastric acid to convert Fe3+ to Fe2+).

blocks.name: Transferrin
blocks.def: The transport form of iron in the blood — iron binds apo-transferrin to form transferrin. Low transferrin (a beta-globulin) means low transport of iron for hemoglobin formation.

blocks.name: Ferritin
blocks.def: The storage form of iron, formed from apo-ferritin plus iron; large stored pools also exist as the less-soluble hemosiderin.

blocks.name: Daily iron loss
blocks.def: About 0.1 mg daily in men, via feces. Women lose considerably more due to menstrual loss, about 1.2 mg daily on average.

blocks.name: Iron absorption regulation (feedback)
blocks.def: Absorption is controlled by apoferritin: when the body's iron stores are full, transferrin becomes saturated, which prevents further mucosal absorption (mucosal cells already loaded with iron simply excrete it in the stool instead of absorbing more). If iron stores are LOW, absorption rate increases roughly 5-fold; if stores are HIGH, absorption rate is reduced — a well-tuned regulatory feedback loop protecting against both deficiency and overload.

blocks.name: Iron overload
blocks.def: Can occur with extreme oral iron intake, or by bypassing the gut's regulatory control entirely via IM or IV iron administration — the gut's protective feedback mechanism only works for oral intake.

blocks.name: RBC lifespan
blocks.def: About 120 days. As cells age, their metabolic processes (which produce the ATP needed to maintain the cell wall) become weaker, making the cells increasingly fragile. They eventually lyse (rupture) as they pass through small passages, especially in the spleen. Lysed cells are phagocytosed by macrophages and Kupffer cells in the spleen and bone marrow.

items: Four protein chains, each holding a haem group with one iron atom — so one haemoglobin carries four oxygen molecules.
HbA is the adult form; HbF (fetal) binds oxygen more tightly, which is how a fetus pulls oxygen from its mother's blood.
That difference matters clinically: HbF persists in some people and softens sickle cell disease.

blocks.name: Hemoglobin structure
blocks.def: Heme (an iron-containing compound) plus 4 polypeptide subunits/chains.

blocks.name: HbA (adult hemoglobin)
blocks.def: Composition α2β2 — the most common form in adults, making up about 96-98% of adult hemoglobin.

blocks.name: HbA2
blocks.def: Composition α2δ2 — a minor adult form, about 2-3% of total.

blocks.name: HbF (fetal hemoglobin)
blocks.def: Composition α2γ2 — the main hemoglobin present in the fetus and newborn, later replaced predominantly by HbA.

sections.title: When Red Cell Numbers Go Wrong

items: Anaemia = too little haemoglobin to carry oxygen adequately. Only three ways it can happen: make too few, lose too many, or destroy too many.
Reduced production — iron, B₁₂ or folate deficiency; marrow failure; kidney disease.
Excessive loss — bleeding, whether obvious or slow and hidden.
Excessive destruction (haemolytic) — sickle cell disease, malaria, incompatible transfusion.
The circulation compensates by working harder: heart rate and output rise, which is why severe anaemia eventually strains the heart.
Polycythemia is the opposite — too many cells, thicker blood, and a higher risk of clotting.
Tiredness, breathlessness on stairs and pale palms are the everyday face of anaemia — oxygen delivery failing, not laziness.
Sickle cell and malaria make this section especially relevant here in Ghana: both destroy red cells, and both present as haemolytic anaemia.

blocks.name: Anemia (general)
blocks.def: A deficiency of normal red blood cells, arising from three broad mechanisms: reduced production, excessive loss, or excessive breakdown.

blocks.name: Anemia from reduced production
blocks.def: Aplastic anemia (bone marrow failure), or nutritional deficiencies — low iron (producing microcytic anemia), low folic acid, or low vitamin B12.

blocks.name: Anemia from excessive loss
blocks.def: Hemorrhage — simply losing blood faster than it can be replaced.

blocks.name: Anemia from excessive breakdown (hemolytic anemia)
blocks.def: Fragile red cells that hemolyze (rupture) too easily, as in hereditary spherocytosis, sickle cell disease (Hemoglobin S), and the thalassemias.

blocks.name: Effects of anemia on the circulatory system
blocks.def: A fall in blood <term d="How thick and sticky a fluid is, and therefore how easily it flows.">viscosity</term> leads to reduced resistance to flow (compounded by vasodilation from tissue hypoxia), increased venous return, INCREASED <term d="The volume of blood the heart pumps out each minute.">cardiac output</term> (extra workload on the heart, trying to compensate for reduced oxygen-carrying capacity), and increased pulse and respiratory rate. Anemia is also reflected in changes to the direct and derived RBC indices (MCH, MCV, MCHC).

blocks.name: Polycythemia
blocks.def: The opposite problem — an abnormal INCREASE in RBC count, arising from: secondary causes like cardiac disease with a right-to-left shunt, physiologic adaptation to high altitude, or a tumor; or from polycythemia rubra vera, a primary bone marrow disorder causing abnormal production of BOTH red cells and white cells.

sections.title: Leucocytes (White Blood Cells) — The Defense Force

items: Far fewer than red cells (~4,000–11,000/µL), but they are the defence force.
Neutrophils — the first responders and most numerous; they eat bacteria and dominate acute infection.
Lymphocytes — the specialists of targeted immunity (antibodies and cell-mediated attack); they rise in viral illness.
Monocytes → macrophages — the big cleaners, handling debris and chronic infection.
Eosinophils — parasites and allergy. Basophils — release histamine, driving allergic responses.
Diapedesis is their defining skill: squeezing out through vessel walls to reach the tissue where the trouble is. Blood is transport, not their workplace.
Pus is essentially dead neutrophils — visible evidence of the first responders having fought and died.
A doctor requesting a differential count is asking the pattern to speak: neutrophils up suggests bacterial, lymphocytes up suggests viral, eosinophils up suggests worms or allergy.

blocks.name: Total WBC count
blocks.def: Normal range about 4,000-11,000 per microliter of blood. Main function: defense.

blocks.name: Granulocytes (general)
blocks.def: Named because staining reveals granular substances in their cytoplasm. Classified by how their granules stain: neutrophils (neutral stain), eosinophils (acid stain), and basophils (basic stain).

blocks.name: Where different leucocytes are found/made
blocks.def: Granulocytes mainly in bone marrow; lymphocytes found some in marrow but more in lymph nodes, thymus, and spleen; monocytes made in bone marrow; platelets also derived in bone marrow (from megakaryocytes).

blocks.title: Next up — meet the cells one by one

items: As you read these, ask one question of each: what is it for, and when does it rise?
Neutrophils → bacteria. Eosinophils → parasites and allergy. Basophils/mast cells → histamine and allergy.
Monocytes → macrophages → the big cleaners. Lymphocytes → targeted, remembering immunity.
That single question turns a list of five cells into a diagnostic tool.

blocks.name: Macrophages
blocks.def: The main mechanism of leucocyte defense: destroying invading organisms via phagocytosis, and processing antibodies and sensitizing lymphocytes to help destroy invaders.

blocks.name: Basophils
blocks.def: Release histamine and heparin — responsible for hypersensitivity reactions such as urticaria (hives), rhinitis, and anaphylactic shock.

blocks.name: Eosinophils
blocks.def: Attack parasites, and are also involved in the allergic process (inactivating mediators of the allergic reaction). Eosinophil levels increase during allergic reactions, making eosinophil count a useful clinical clue.

blocks.name: Neutrophils
blocks.def: Ingest and kill bacteria, and are responsible for the formation of pus. Average half-life in circulation is only about 6 hours, requiring high daily production to maintain blood levels.

blocks.name: Diapedesis
blocks.def: The process by which white blood cells migrate from the bloodstream into surrounding tissues by squeezing between endothelial cells lining the blood vessels. Neutrophils use diapedesis to enter tissues — most neutrophils that enter the gut are simply lost there. During bacterial invasion, the resulting inflammatory response stimulates the bone marrow, and neutrophils are attracted to the site of infection by chemotaxis, while other factors 'opsonize' (coat) bacteria with IgG so they can be more easily engulfed by phagocytosis.

blocks.name: Monocytes
blocks.def: Circulate in the blood for about 72 hours before entering tissues, where they become tissue macrophages — including Kupffer cells (in the liver) and pulmonary alveolar macrophages (in the lungs). This whole network is now called the Tissue Macrophage System (formerly called the Reticuloendothelial System). These cells are attracted to bacteria by chemotaxis and then engulf and kill them.

blocks.name: Lymphocytes
blocks.def: Main roles: producing antibodies, and 'remembering' a previous exposure to a pathogen (immunological memory). Involved in both humoral immunity and cellular immunity.

blocks.title: Next up — the two lymphocyte families

items: T cells attack infected cells directly and coordinate the response — T for Thymus, where they mature.
B cells make antibodies — B for Bone marrow.
Simple split: T cells do the fighting in person; B cells send weapons.

blocks.name: T-lymphocytes
blocks.def: Responsible for reactions to foreign protein, delayed allergic reactions, and rejection of foreign (transplanted) tissue.

blocks.name: B-lymphocytes
blocks.def: Mediate antibody production, differentiating into plasma cells to do so.

blocks.title: Next up — two styles of defence

items: Non-specific (innate) — fast, general, no memory. It attacks anything foreign.
Specific (adaptive) — slower to start, precisely targeted, and it remembers.
That memory is the entire basis of vaccination: teach the specific system now, so it responds instantly later.

blocks.name: Non-specific immune response
blocks.def: Protects against foreign substances WITHOUT needing to recognize their specific identity — a generic, broad defense.

blocks.name: Specific immune response
blocks.def: Depends on RECOGNITION of the specific substance or cell to be attacked — a targeted, identity-based defense.

blocks.name: Mast cells
blocks.def: Differentiate from basophils (a tissue-resident counterpart to circulating basophils).

items: Agglutinogens (antigens) sit on the red cell surface; agglutinins (antibodies) float in the plasma. You never carry the antibody against your own antigen.
So: A has anti-B; B has anti-A; AB has neither; O has both.
O = universal donor (no antigens to be attacked). AB = universal recipient (no antibodies to attack anything).
Give the wrong group and the recipient's antibodies clump and burst the donor cells — potentially fatal, which is why cross-matching is non-negotiable.
Rhesus (Rh) is separate: Rh-negative people make anti-D only after exposure, not automatically.
That delay explains haemolytic disease of the newborn: an Rh-negative mother sensitised by a first Rh-positive baby attacks the next one. Anti-D immunoglobulin prevents it.
Blood group is written on donor cards and checked repeatedly before transfusion because a mismatch is one of the fastest ways to kill a patient in hospital.
Anti-D given to Rh-negative mothers is one of the great quiet successes of modern medicine — a preventable tragedy, prevented.

blocks.name: Agglutinogens
blocks.def: Membrane antigens on the surface of red blood cells. The most important are the A and B agglutinogens, which are used to classify blood into the A, B, AB, or O groups, depending on which agglutinogen(s) are present on the red cell.

blocks.name: Agglutinins
blocks.def: Antibodies (of the IgM class) that exist against agglutinogens NOT present on a person's own red cells — the body naturally produces antibodies against whichever ABO antigens it lacks.

blocks.name: ABO blood group system
blocks.def: Type A has A agglutinogen and anti-B agglutinin. Type B has B agglutinogen and anti-A agglutinin. Type AB has BOTH A and B agglutinogens and NEITHER agglutinin. Type O has NEITHER agglutinogen and BOTH anti-A and anti-B agglutinins.

blocks.name: Universal recipient
blocks.def: Blood type AB — because AB individuals have no agglutinins (anti-A or anti-B) at all, they can theoretically receive blood from any ABO group without an ABO-mismatch reaction.

blocks.name: Universal donor
blocks.def: Blood type O — because O red cells carry NEITHER A nor B agglutinogen, they won't trigger an ABO-antibody reaction in a recipient of any blood type.

blocks.name: Transfusion compatibility testing
blocks.def: Practically requires 'group and cross match' testing before any transfusion — determining the recipient's blood group and directly testing donor and recipient blood together for compatibility, since dilution of agglutinins from the donor is also an important practical consideration.

blocks.name: Abnormal transfusion reactions
blocks.def: Incompatibility triggers agglutination (clumping) and hemolysis (rupture) of red cells, which can then cause anemia, jaundice, renal tubular damage, and potentially renal failure.

blocks.name: Rhesus (Rh) factor
blocks.def: Many Rh antigens exist, but the most clinically important is antigen D. Rh-POSITIVE individuals have agglutinogen D but no natural antibody against it. Rh-NEGATIVE individuals lack agglutinogen D, but importantly, they have the CAPACITY to form anti-D agglutinin if they are ever exposed to D-positive red cells.

blocks.name: Hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis)
blocks.def: Occurs when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby (inherited from an Rh-positive father). The mother's anti-D antibody (IgG, small enough to cross the placenta) crosses into fetal circulation, causing agglutination and hemolysis IN UTERO — leading to fetal anemia, jaundice, kernicterus (bilirubin damage to the basal ganglia), and potentially heart failure (hydrops fetalis).

blocks.name: Anti-D antibody (Rh immunoglobulin) as prevention
blocks.def: Given to Rh-negative mothers during the postpartum period specifically to PREVENT the mother's own immune system from forming anti-D antibodies in response to any fetal Rh-positive cells that entered her circulation during delivery — protecting any future Rh-positive pregnancies from the same risk.

items: Hemostasis = stopping bleeding, in three overlapping steps.
1. Vasoconstriction — the vessel narrows immediately, reducing flow to the injury.
2. Platelet plug — platelets stick to exposed collagen, become activated, and recruit more platelets. A fast, temporary patch.
3. Coagulation — a fibrin mesh converts that soft plug into a firm clot.
Healthy endothelium is actively non-stick — it releases prostacyclin to repel platelets. Clotting begins when that smooth lining is broken.
Note the design: the default is not to clot, and clotting is what happens when the lining is damaged.
A small cut: bleeding slows within seconds (vasoconstriction), a soft plug forms in a minute or two (platelets), and a proper scab sets later (fibrin). You watch all three stages happen.

blocks.x: The moment a blood vessel is injured, your body launches a rapid, tightly-choreographed sequence: first the vessel clamps down, then platelets rush in and stick together, and finally a mesh of protein fiber locks everything in place. Get the timing or balance wrong in either direction — too little clotting, or too much — and the consequences can be equally dangerous.

blocks.name: Hemostasis (definition)
blocks.def: The elimination of bleeding — literally, 'stopping blood.'

blocks.name: Sources of bleeding and their hemostatic challenge
blocks.def: Arterioles, capillaries, and venules. Hemostatic mechanisms are most effective for these smaller vessels; bigger arteries are much harder to stop bleeding from without external intervention. Venous bleeding usually stops relatively more easily because of the lower pressure in veins. The body maintains a careful BALANCE of clotting versus anti-clotting features to prevent unwanted clotting inside intact vessels (intravascular coagulation).

blocks.name: Vasoconstriction (local hemostatic response)
blocks.def: Contraction of smooth muscle in the injured vessel wall reduces blood flow to the region — the first, immediate response to injury, before any clot has even begun forming.

blocks.name: Endothelial surface adhesion
blocks.def: Endothelial surfaces stick together after coming into contact, aided by serotonin and other vasoconstrictors released at the injury site.

blocks.name: Platelet plug
blocks.def: Forms to seal the defect in the blood vessel wall. Platelets are derived from megakaryocytes (giant cells in the bone marrow) and aggregate (clump together) at the injury site when stimulated.

blocks.name: Stimuli for platelet aggregation
blocks.def: Collagen fibers exposed from the vessel wall, ADP secreted from platelets' own secretory granules as they begin aggregating, thromboxane A2 (formed from arachidonic acid in platelets — its formation is famously INHIBITED by aspirin), von Willebrand factor (produced by endothelial cells and platelets, forming a bridge between the vessel wall and the first layer of platelets by binding both collagen and platelets), thrombin, and platelet-activating factor (from endothelial cells).

blocks.name: Prostacyclin
blocks.def: An inhibitor of platelet aggregation, produced in the vessel wall (adventitia), that OPPOSES the action of thromboxane A2 — keeping platelet activation localized to the actual injury site and preventing unwanted clot formation in otherwise normal, healthy vessels.

items: A clot is physically simple: a mesh of fibrin threads with blood cells trapped in it — like a net catching fish.
The cascade is a chain of activations: each factor switches on the next. It is amplification (Topic 02) again — a tiny trigger becomes a decisive response.
Intrinsic pathway — triggered by contact with damaged surfaces (all components already in the blood); slower.
Extrinsic pathway — triggered by tissue factor from injured tissue; much faster.
Both converge on a common pathway: activate factor X → prothrombin becomes thrombin → fibrinogen becomes fibrin.
The cascade design is deliberate: many steps mean many control points, so the process can be regulated and stopped.
It is a line of dominoes again — one nudge, a big decisive result, and several places where you can remove a domino to halt it.
Most anticoagulant drugs work precisely by removing one domino.

blocks.cap: The intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge into the common clotting pathway.

blocks.name: Blood clot
blocks.def: A protective mechanism preventing excessive blood loss after injury — formed by the transformation of blood into a solid gel, via the conversion of the protein fibrinogen into fibrin monomers, which then polymerize into an insoluble mesh.

blocks.name: What a clot actually is, physically
blocks.def: A tough, insoluble, polymerized fibrin protein network that forms around the platelets already stuck at the wound edge. This network entangles blood cells and then contracts, squeezing out serum and leaving behind a clot, which dries into a scab — preventing further blood loss AND preventing bacteria from entering the wound. Normal clotting takes place within about 5 minutes.

blocks.name: The 12 classical clotting factors (Roman numeral system)
blocks.def: I - Fibrinogen, II - Prothrombin, III - Thromboplastin, IV - Calcium, V - Labile Factor, VII - Stable Factor, VIII - Antihemophilic Factor A, IX - Christmas Factor, X - Stuart-Prower Factor, XI - Plasma Thromboplastin Antecedent, XII - Hageman Factor, XIII - Fibrin Stabilizing Factor. (Note: there is traditionally no Factor VI in the numbering system.)

blocks.name: Intrinsic pathway
blocks.def: Activated by trauma INSIDE the vascular system — triggered by platelets, exposed endothelium, chemicals, or collagen. This pathway is SLOWER than the extrinsic pathway, but considered more important overall. Involves factors XII, XI, IX, and VIII.

blocks.name: Extrinsic pathway
blocks.def: Activated by the introduction of tissue factor from crushed or injured tissue (a protein 'extrinsic' — external — to blood itself) — this pathway forms a fibrin clot RAPIDLY. Involves factors V, VII, and XIII.

blocks.name: The clotting cascade — converging point
blocks.def: Both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge on a COMMON pathway: activation of Factor X (Xa), which (with Factor V, platelet phospholipids, and Ca2+) converts prothrombin to thrombin. Thrombin then converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and Factor XIII stabilizes the fibrin mesh.

sections.title: Keeping Clotting in Check — Anticoagulation & Fibrinolysis

items: If clotting were unopposed, one small injury could clot your entire circulation — so the brakes matter as much as the accelerator.
Antithrombin III neutralises thrombin; thrombomodulin and protein C switch off amplification; prostacyclin keeps platelets away from healthy lining.
Fibrinolysis is the clean-up crew: plasmin dissolves fibrin once the vessel has healed.

The drugs map onto these steps: aspirin blocks platelet aggregation; heparin boosts antithrombin III (works instantly, in vitro too); warfarin blocks vitamin-K-dependent factor production (slow, in vivo only); streptokinase actively dissolves an existing clot.
Worth holding: aspirin and heparin prevent; streptokinase destroys.
A daily low-dose aspirin after a heart attack is this section in a tablet — making platelets slightly less sticky, for years.
Warfarin patients need regular blood tests and must watch their diet because vitamin K in food directly opposes the drug.

blocks.name: Anticoagulation mechanisms (overview)
blocks.def: The body prevents excessive clotting and breaks down excess clots by producing only a limited amount of clotting factors, and via specific regulatory proteins like antithrombin III.

blocks.name: Antithrombin III
blocks.def: A circulating protease inhibitor that blocks the activity of several clotting factors by binding to them — IX, X, XI, and the active form of XII. Its activity is greatly facilitated by heparin, which aids the binding of antithrombin III to these target factors.

blocks.name: Thrombomodulin and Protein C
blocks.def: Endothelial cells (except in the central microcirculation) produce thrombomodulin. Protein C is a naturally occurring anticoagulant that (once activated) also inactivates inhibitors of tissue plasminogen activator — indirectly promoting clot breakdown.

blocks.name: The fibrinolytic system
blocks.def: Produces plasmin (also called fibrinolysin), which breaks down fibrin into fibrin degradation products — this is the system responsible for dissolving clots once they're no longer needed.

blocks.name: Principles of anticoagulant drugs
blocks.def: Anticoagulants work by one of four strategies: preventing formation of clotting factors, preventing activation or action of a clotting factor, preventing platelet aggregation, or breaking down an existing clot.

blocks.name: Aspirin (as an anticoagulant)
blocks.def: Reduces thromboxane A2 formation, thereby reducing platelet aggregation — used clinically to prevent or reduce clot formation and thus help prevent heart disease.

blocks.name: Heparin (as an anticoagulant)
blocks.def: Blocks the action of factors IX, X, XI, and XII by aiding antithrombin III's binding to them. Heparin's action can itself be INACTIVATED by protamine, which binds heparin and prevents it from enhancing antithrombin III's anticoagulant effect — the clinical 'reversal agent' for heparin.

blocks.name: Warfarin (dicoumarol)
blocks.def: Inhibits the action of vitamin K, which is required for the synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as the anticoagulant proteins C and S.

blocks.name: Streptokinase
blocks.def: A clot-dissolving (thrombolytic) drug, used to actively break down an already-formed clot — different in strategy from aspirin, heparin, and warfarin, which all work to PREVENT further clotting rather than dissolve existing clots.

items: Two directions of failure: bleeding too easily or clotting when you should not.
Liver disease causes bleeding because the liver makes most clotting factors.
Thrombocytopenic purpura = too few platelets; thromboasthenic purpura = enough platelets that do not work properly.
Von Willebrand disease — platelets cannot stick properly. Haemophilia A — missing factor VIII, so the cascade stalls.
Thrombus = a clot formed in the wrong place. Embolus = a piece that breaks off and travels until it blocks something.
That distinction is clinically everything: a thrombus is a local problem; an embolus is a travelling one, causing stroke or pulmonary embolism.
Long flights and long bus journeys are a real risk because still legs mean sluggish flow, and sluggish flow favours clotting.
In haemophilia, the danger is not the visible cut — it is bleeding into joints and muscles, because the plug forms but never sets firm.

blocks.name: Liver disease and clotting
blocks.def: The liver is essential for both absorbing vitamin K (which requires bile) and synthesizing plasma clotting proteins — liver disease can therefore impair clotting via reduced vitamin K absorption AND reduced synthesis of clotting factors.

blocks.name: Thrombocytopenic purpura
blocks.def: Abnormally LOW levels of platelets, causing easy bruising and multiple subcutaneous hemorrhages.

blocks.name: Thromboasthenic purpura
blocks.def: ABNORMAL (dysfunctional) platelets, rather than low numbers — the platelets are present but don't function correctly.

blocks.name: Von Willebrand factor deficiency
blocks.def: Causes a lack of platelet aggregation, since von Willebrand factor is what bridges platelets to the injured vessel wall and to each other.

blocks.name: Hemophilia A
blocks.def: Caused by a lack of Factor VIII (the antihemophilic factor). The gene is located on the X chromosome (X-linked inheritance). Historically treated by replacing the missing factor with a plasma fraction containing Factor VIII (which carried a risk of transmitting infections like HIV/AIDS from donor blood before modern screening) — now increasingly treated using genetically engineered factor VIII, avoiding that risk.

blocks.name: Thrombus
blocks.def: An abnormal blood clot that forms INSIDE a vessel, often due to changes in the inner vessel wall (e.g., arteriosclerotic plaques) or sluggish blood flow — a particular risk in veins, especially during prolonged prostration (bed rest) or the postoperative period.

blocks.name: Embolus
blocks.def: A thrombus (or part of one) that breaks away from its original site and travels through the circulation, potentially lodging elsewhere and blocking a vessel at a distant location.

items: Bleeding time tests platelets and the vessel response — the first, quick phase.
Clotting time tests the cascade — the slower fibrin phase.
That distinction is the point: they test two different stages, so an abnormal result tells you where the fault is.
Prothrombin time (PT) assesses the extrinsic and common pathways, and is the standard monitor for warfarin.
Samples are kept liquid for testing using anticoagulants such as citrate or EDTA, which bind calcium — a neat proof that calcium is essential to clotting.
The purple-topped bottle used for a full blood count contains EDTA — it works by taking calcium away from the cascade.

blocks.name: Bleeding time vs clotting time
blocks.def: Bleeding from a minor wound typically ceases BEFORE a clot is even fully formed — meaning bleeding time is normally SHORTER than clotting time. These are two separate lab tests measuring different aspects of hemostasis.

blocks.name: Bleeding time (test)
blocks.def: Denotes deficiencies in platelets, extrinsic pathway factors, or vascular disorders. Measured classically at the earlobe, normally 3-6 minutes, and may be affected by the degree of hyperemia (blood flow to the area) and the nature of the cut.

blocks.name: Clotting time (test)
blocks.def: Reflects reductions in factors II, V, VII, IX, X, XI, or XII — i.e., abnormalities of the intrinsic and common pathways. Measured by collecting blood in a clean test tube and agitating it for 30 seconds until clotting occurs, normally 5-8 minutes; results depend on tube size, so the test must be standardized. Prolonged in hemophiliacs.

blocks.name: Preventing blood from clotting during collection
blocks.def: Blood collection tubes contain substances like oxalate, citrate, or heparin, which remove or reduce available Ca2+ (oxalate/citrate) or block the clotting cascade directly (heparin) — since calcium is an essential clotting factor (Factor IV), removing it prevents the sample from clotting in the tube.

blocks.name: Prothrombin time (PT)
blocks.def: Estimates the total quantity of functional prothrombin. Procedure: take a sample, add oxalate to remove Ca2+ (preventing clotting), then add Ca2+ back along with tissue thromboplastin to specifically initiate the EXTRINSIC pathway, and check the time it takes to clot. Normal value approximately 12 seconds.

items: Serum = plasma − clotting factors.
O = universal donor (no antigens); AB = universal recipient (no antibodies).
Extrinsic = external tissue damage = fast; intrinsic = everything already inside = slower.
Bleeding time tests platelets; clotting time tests the cascade.
B₁₂/folate → large cells; iron → small pale cells.
Aspirin and heparin prevent; streptokinase dissolves.

blocks.title: Cleared up — the confusions that cost marks

items: Anaemia is not simply 'low blood'. It is insufficient haemoglobin to carry oxygen — a person can have a normal volume and still be anaemic.
ABO antibodies exist without exposure; Rh antibodies form only after exposure. That difference is the whole reason haemolytic disease of the newborn spares the first baby.
Thrombus vs embolus: a thrombus forms and stays; an embolus travels. Same clot, different danger.
Clotting is not the default. Healthy endothelium actively prevents it — clotting begins when that lining is broken.
← Body Fluids (Topic 01): plasma is the ECF inside vessels, and albumin's osmotic pull is what decides how water is shared between plasma and tissue.
← Homeostasis (Topic 02): clotting is the textbook example of positive feedback with a definite end point; the anticoagulant brakes are the negative feedback that contains it.
← Cardiac & Smooth Muscle (Topics 05–06): the pump and the vessel tone that move this tissue around the body.
→ Autonomic Nervous System (Topic 09): vessel calibre, and therefore blood pressure and flow distribution, are under autonomic control.
The one-line summary: a liquid tissue that carries and defends — and whose clotting system must be fast enough to save you and restrained enough not to kill you.

lines: Let blood clot and what is left has lost fibrinogen and the factors consumed in clotting — that single line answers a whole family of questions.
Blood is roughly 55% plasma and 45% cells, and makes up about 8% of body weight — near 5 litres in an average adult.
Neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils — the white cells in descending order of how many you normally have.
A red cell lasts about 120 days, a circulating neutrophil about 6 hours, and a monocyte about 72 hours before it settles into tissue as a macrophage.
Tissue damage outside the vessel triggers the quick extrinsic route; the intrinsic pathway uses only what is already in the blood and takes longer.
